# First pass: guess before you read

Nothing here is scored, and you can redo any answer. Answer all five first; the explanations follow. A wrong guess still helps.

## Prompt 1: the spacing chart

Each column is one frame, numbered 1 to 12. Height goes from 0, on the floor, up to 10, where the ball is let go. A dot can sit between two lines.

Here is how to read the chart, filled in with the same gap on every frame:

![A spacing chart with twelve evenly spaced dots stepping down from 10 to 0](asset:spacing_how_to_read)

Even gaps look like an escalator, not a ball falling. Make yours fall like a real ball.

On paper instead: draw 12 upright lines, mark heights 0 to 10 up the side, and put one dot on each line.

**Why guess first?** An answer you work out for yourself, even a wrong one, sticks better than the same sentence read off a page. In one set of five experiments, people who took a short test before reading a passage scored higher overall on the final test than people who only read it (Pan and Sana, 2021; the full list is at the end of this module).

**If this feels harder than being told,** that feeling is normal and it is not a sign that it is going badly. Students in classes that make them work things out learned more, and felt they had learned less, than students in lectures (Deslauriers and colleagues, 2019).

**If you would rather read first,** you can open every explanation at once. Guessing first is the method, not a rule.
